title: I fixed a tractor using John Deere’s self-repair service. Farmers aren’t sold on it.
gist: A year after launching its Pro Service self-repair software, John Deere has only about 1,000 daily users out of roughly 1.8 million US farms, and farmers, litigation, and right-to-repair advocates argue the $99M settlement and FTC deal haven't changed a business model where dealer-gated diagnostics, PIP-based fixes, and steep subscription pricing still push power toward the company over equipment owners.

insights.claim: A year after launch, John Deere's Pro Service self-repair software has about a thousand daily users, a very small figure given there are roughly 1.8 million farms in the United States.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: Sub-0.1% daily-active penetration after a year signals the self-repair software rollout is failing to gain real-world traction despite being John Deere's flagship response to right-to-repair pressure, a weak proof point if regulators or courts revisit adequacy of the settlement remedies.
insights.quote: A year on, John Deere says its service has about a thousand daily users—a relatively small number, given that there are somewhere around 1.8 million farms in the US.

insights.claim: John Deere product manager Kelli Sullivan says the company is still primarily focused on 'getting the word out' about tools that are already available to customers, implying awareness rather than product capability is the main adoption barrier.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: If the company's own framing is an awareness gap rather than a product or trust gap, that is a testable claim; farmer testimony in the same article contradicts it, suggesting the real barrier is deeper distrust rather than marketing.
insights.quote: We’re just trying to get the word out

insights.claim: Missouri farmer and named plaintiff Jared Wilson does not use Pro Service and does not know anyone who does; he says farmers he knows instead use cracked, gray-market versions of diagnostic software rather than pay John Deere.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: Widespread use of pirated diagnostic tools instead of the paid official product is a direct signal that pricing and trust, not feature gaps, are driving farmers away from Deere's monetized self-repair channel.
insights.locator: Wilson does not use Pro Service

insights.claim: John Deere's Pro Service, introduced in 2025, starts at $195 per year for an individual machine, while full-fleet access for larger operations or independent repair shops starts at $4,995 per year, and agricultural-and-turf service access costs $5,995 per year.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: These are concrete recurring-revenue subscription price points for Deere's software/diagnostics business, relevant to modeling the company's shift toward services revenue and to gauging affordability friction for small farms and independent repair shops.

insights.claim: Pro Service connects to equipment via Wi-Fi or cable, uses the machine's serial number to pull manual instructions and diagnostic data, offers some offline-capable features, and links directly to John Deere's parts shop for needed replacement parts.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: Direct in-app links to Deere's own parts store show the self-repair tool doubles as a captive e-commerce funnel, reinforcing a closed-loop parts/service revenue model rather than opening the ecosystem to third parties.
insights.quote: It feels as smooth as scrolling through an Amazon page.
insights.locator: Pro Service lets owners connect Deere’s software

insights.claim: John Deere has added an AI chatbot called 'JD' to its Operations Center self-repair tool, intended to make it easier for users to find information about machine components.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: Another example of AI chat interfaces being layered onto legacy industrial diagnostic/support software, a pattern worth tracking across equipment and industrial-software vendors adding AI support-agent features.
insights.locator: John Deere also recently introduced an AI chatbot

insights.claim: Modern John Deere tractors can have upward of 50 electronic controllers as machines grow in size and complexity, according to CTO Jahmy Hindman.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: Rising controller count per machine quantifies why agricultural equipment increasingly resembles software-defined vehicles, raising the technical bar (and dealer dependency) for any repair, official or independent.
insights.quote: As the tractor products grow in size, they also grow in number of controllers that are necessary in order to make it all work

insights.claim: In April, John Deere agreed to pay a $99 million settlement to equipment owners over burdensome repair costs, and in July it settled a separate FTC lawsuit requiring the company to make its products more repairable; the company admitted no wrongdoing in either case and neither settlement is yet final pending a judge's ruling.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: Two concurrent legal actions (private class action plus FTC enforcement) against the same practices signal sustained regulatory and litigation risk for John Deere's repair-restriction business model, a cost and reputational overhang to monitor through final court rulings.
insights.locator: That frustration has manifested in multiple lawsuits

insights.claim: Repair advocates argue that both the $99 million settlement and the FTC settlement are insufficient in financial terms and unlikely to actually change John Deere's underlying repair-restriction behavior.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: Advocate skepticism that legal settlements will change conduct suggests John Deere may face further legal or legislative action if voluntary/court-mandated fixes remain shallow.
insights.locator: Repair advocates say the two measures

insights.claim: Named plaintiff Jared Wilson calls the $99 million settlement 'fundamentally flawed' and is skeptical that John Deere's current self-repair concessions represent genuine change, comparing the company's promises to a fraudulent land sale.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: A lead plaintiff's public distrust of the settlement outcome itself is a signal that legal remedies achieved so far may not satisfy the underlying farmer base, raising odds of continued advocacy, press scrutiny, or further legal challenges.
insights.quote: If you believe what they’re saying now—that this is actually it and we’re getting everything we’ve asked for—then I’ve got some oceanfront property in Arizona to sell you.
insights.locator: Jared Wilson quote on settlement credibility

themes.theme: Structural limits of the self-repair model

insights.claim: John Deere's diagnostic system relies on Product Improvement Plans (PIPs) that are only issued after the company has gathered enough field data to confirm a problem, meaning a farmer encountering a genuinely novel issue has no official fix guidance until Deere verifies and formally documents it.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: This reactive, centrally-gated update process structurally guarantees a lag for novel failures, meaning the self-repair tool cannot function as true independent diagnostics for cutting-edge problems, a core limitation for any 'self-repair' claim.
insights.locator: Part of the problem are PIPs

insights.claim: Farmer Jared Wilson says Pro Service works best only for simple repairs and becomes unworkable when a machine throws multiple simultaneous diagnostic codes, since there's no clear way to know where to start troubleshooting.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: Confirms the tool's practical utility is confined to low-complexity fixes, meaning it doesn't reduce dependency on dealer technicians for the harder, more costly repair jobs that matter most economically.
insights.quote: If you have three different or four different diagnostic codes, where do you start in the tree to figure out what’s wrong?
insights.locator: Jared Wilson quote on multiple failures

insights.claim: Wilson says it is almost impossible to verify that the customer-facing version of Deere's diagnostic software has full feature parity with the dealer version, even though CTO Jahmy Hindman claims the versions are identical.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: An unverifiable parity claim from the manufacturer, disputed implicitly by a farmer plaintiff, is exactly the kind of asymmetric-information problem that fuels ongoing right-to-repair litigation and distrust.

insights.claim: Repair.org board member Willie Cade argues John Deere behaves as a monopolist whose real customer is Wall Street, not the farmer.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: This framing crystallizes the investor-relevant tension directly: locked-down repair and recurring software fees exist to serve margin/shareholder interests, meaning right-to-repair reform is a potential structural risk to a high-margin parts-and-service revenue stream.
insights.quote: Their real customer is not the farmer. Their real customer is Wall Street.

insights.claim: Jared Wilson frames the John Deere repair fight as the leading edge of a much broader societal battle over the right to repair that extends to every category of personal device, not just agricultural equipment.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: Positions John Deere's case as a bellwether: legal or legislative outcomes here could set precedent affecting right-to-repair rules across consumer electronics, vehicles, and other durable goods sectors.
insights.quote: But it’s really the vanguard of a much bigger and persistent problem that affects every aspect of our society.

themes.theme: Growing autonomy and connectivity of equipment

insights.claim: Many newer John Deere machines are equipped with 4G wireless connections enabling collection of precise location data and other operating metrics, and some tractors can run fully autonomously on predetermined paths without a human operator.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: Combines two structurally significant trends — pervasive telemetry data collection and creeping machine autonomy in agriculture — both of which raise the stakes of who controls diagnostic/repair access as equipment becomes more software-dependent.
